source.title: Hypothesis Testing the Circuit Hypothesis in LLMs
source.authors: Claudia Shi; Nicolas Beltran-Velez; Achille Nazaret; Carolina Zheng; Adrià Garriga-Alonso; Andrew Jesson; Maggie Makar; D. Blei

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates the IOI circuit identified in the original work on GPT-2 small, using circuit knockouts, edge removals, and IOI task scores. Its hypothesis-testing framework and faithfulness metric differ from the original criteria, but it directly tests the candidate circuit and its effects on IOI.
record.gate_note: The IOI-specific results below are included. Results for the other five circuits and other tasks are not findings about the IOI circuit. Citations to the original IOI study are not counted as results.
record.test_reason: The study re-evaluates the Wang et al. IOI circuit in GPT-2 small with the original IOI data, STR patching and logit-difference score. It uses a new hypothesis-testing framework (equivalence, HSIC independence, edge-level minimality, sufficiency and partial necessity against random circuits) aimed at the same faithfulness, completeness and minimality questions. That makes it a different method on the same question (T2), not a same-method replication (T1).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely, the IOI circuit fails all three idealized tests (equivalence, independence, minimality), yet is far from a random subnetwork in the sufficiency and partial-necessity tests. About 20% of its edges can be removed without losing faithfulness. Knockdown alone is insufficient to judge circuit quality, especially under STR ablation, and results may not generalize across experimental setups.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates the original IOI candidate circuit using the IOI task and STR patching setup, but frames evaluation with its own hypothesis tests and ℓ2 faithfulness metric. It also tests edge minimality and compares STR with zero-ablation knockdown behavior.
record.method_sensitivity: Knockdown conclusions differ between STR and zero ablation. The authors also state that knockdown alone can be insufficient and sensitive to artifacts from the validation dataset. Prompt-distribution effects are not experimentally compared.
record.problems: The paper notes that its tests use a fixed experimental setup and that conclusions may differ across setups. The reported table for the equivalence test appears inconsistent with the appendix narrative and the IOI proportion of 0.24. No controlled comparison across prompt distributions is reported.

untested.parts: The 26-head, 7-class structure and the roles of individual head classes are not examined; only the edge-level circuit as a whole is tested.
All: backup name-mover takeover after ablation is not tested.
All: only GPT-2 small is used; no other models, sizes, checkpoints, or component reuse across tasks.
All: no alternative circuit-finding method is run and no circuit is recovered under another ablation. The STR versus zero-ablation contrast concerns the knockdown evaluation, not circuit recovery.
Prompt-distribution dependence and alternative faithfulness metrics (only ℓ2 is used) are not tested.
All: no name orders, templates or more-name variants.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The record's V4 labels were dropped because the STR versus zero-ablation result concerns the evaluation (V5), not whether methods recover the same circuit. Table 1's caption says ✓ means 'null rejected', but the cells actually mean 'passes', so the IOI fail entries are consistent with the text. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates the IOI candidate circuit's faithfulness, knockdown, and minimality, but does not test the stated roles of individual head classes or confirm the 26-head, 7-class description.
Backup-head takeover after ablating main name-mover heads is not tested.
The IOI circuit is evaluated only in GPT-2 small; other models, sizes, checkpoints, and component reuse for other tasks are not tested.
The paper compares STR and zero ablation for knockdown effects, but does not compare circuit-finding methods or establish that other methods recover the same circuit.
The paper reports sensitivity to ablation choice and limitations of the knockdown metric, but does not run a controlled comparison across prompt distributions.
Other name orders, templates, and sentences with more names are not evaluated.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared the IOI candidate circuit's task score with the full model; reported the proportion of inputs on which the circuit outperformed the model.
rows.measure: Proportion of inputs where the candidate circuit outperforms the full model
rows.note: The authors state that none of the natural circuits passed the equivalence test. The paper's Table 1 appears inconsistent with this account: it marks the IOI equivalence null as retained, while § E.1 says none passed and reports 0.24. The reported proportion is recorded here without resolving that discrepancy.
rows.check: The record's 'inconsistency' note is a misreading. Table 1's cells use ✓ for passing (Induction ✓ on independence and minimality, matching the text). IOI's × therefore means it fails equivalence, consistent with §E.1; only the caption wording is off. The circuit beats the model on only 24% of inputs (ϵ=0.1 would require 40–60%), so faithfulness is partial for V1. For V5, this row shows the circuit explains only part of the behaviour.

source_check.locator_found: § E.1, Table 3: IOI proportion 0.24; none of the natural circuits passed equivalence.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Knocked out the candidate circuit and tested whether its score on the task was independent of the full model's score using HSIC.
rows.baseline: Independence between complement-circuit and full-model task scores
rows.note: The test rejects independence, which the paper interprets as evidence that knocking out the candidate circuit does not remove all task-relevant information.
rows.check: Independence is rejected (HSIC 0.001, p=0.01): the complement still carries task information. For V1 completeness this is partial. For V5 it shows the circuit does not capture all task-relevant computation.

source_check.locator_found: § E.2, Table 4: IOI HSIC 0.001, p-value 0.01; § 3.1 defines complement independence.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Removed candidate-circuit edges individually and compared each score change with changes from removing sampled edges in inflated circuits.
rows.measure: Change in task score after edge removal relative to the inflated-circuit reference distribution
rows.baseline: Randomly added edges in inflated circuits
rows.value: The IOI circuit fails the minimality test; a few edges can be removed with little impact.
rows.note: The authors classify the IOI circuit as non-minimal and report that some of its edges have little effect when removed.
rows.check: The recorded state described the non-minimality finding, not the V1 claim. Relative to V1's minimality criterion it is partial: the circuit fails the edge-level minimality test, but only 'a few edges' are removable, which the authors say agrees with Wang et al. This is an edge-level test, unlike Wang's node-level one. V5 link removed: the row does not concern evaluation sensitivity.

source_check.locator_found: § 3.1 Minimality specifies inflated-circuit references and Bonferroni correction; § 4.1 and § E.3 specify q*=0.9; § E.3 and Figure 5 report removable IOI edges.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Gradually removed edges from the canonical IOI circuit, beginning with edges ranked least minimal.
rows.value: About 20% of the edges can be removed while retaining the same faithfulness.
rows.note: The authors also report that IOI faithfulness does not vary monotonically as more edges are removed.
rows.check: About 20% of edges can be removed with unchanged faithfulness, and faithfulness varies non-monotonically. This bears on V1 minimality. The V5 link is weak and is removed.

rows.subject: GPT-2 small
rows.operation_detail: Compared candidate-circuit knockdown effects under STR ablation with the effects of knocking down increasingly large random circuits.

conditions.value: increased up to the complete model

rows.baseline: Knockdown effects of random circuits, including the complete model
rows.value: The candidate circuit's knockdown remains more significant; knocking down the complete model has less impact than knocking down the candidate circuit.
rows.note: The authors describe this pattern as specific to STR ablation and warn that the knockdown metric is sensitive to validation-dataset artifacts.
rows.check: V4 link removed: V4 concerns whether other methods or ablations recover the same circuit. This row shows that a knockdown evaluation outcome depends on the ablation. Under STR, knocking out the whole model hurts less than knocking out the circuit, which the authors call a validation-dataset artifact.

source_check.locator_found: § 4.2 Partial necessity test: under STR, complete-model knockout has less impact than candidate knockout for IOI and G-T; relative significance remains constant as reference size increases.

rows.operation_detail: Compared candidate-circuit knockdown effects under zero ablation with the effects of knocking down increasingly large random circuits.
rows.baseline: Knockdown effects of random circuits as their size increases
rows.value: The candidate circuit's relative significance decreases monotonically as random-circuit size increases; the STR pattern is absent.
rows.note: The contrast with STR is the reported ablation-choice sensitivity.
rows.check: V4 link removed, as for R8. Under zero ablation the circuit's relative significance falls monotonically. This is the contrast that shows the evaluation's sensitivity to ablation choice.

source_check.locator_found: § 4.2 Partial necessity test: under zero ablation, candidate relative significance decreases monotonically as random-circuit size increases.

relationships.condition: Sufficiency and partial-necessity tests against random reference circuits, STR ablation, ℓ2 faithfulness
relationships.reason: The IOI circuit is significantly more faithful than random circuits at 90% of model size, and knocking it out is worse than knocking out same-size random circuits drawn from the complement or the model (R4, R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: The circuit was significantly more faithful than random circuits occupying 90% of model size, and its knockout caused more damage than equal-size random knockouts.

source_check.condition: Sufficiency and partial-necessity tests against random reference circuits, STR ablation, ℓ2 faithfulness
source_check.reason: R4–R6 establish relative faithfulness and task relevance against random circuits, providing support for the circuit under these flexible criteria.

relationships.condition: Stringent idealized tests: equivalence, independence, edge-level minimality
relationships.reason: The circuit beats the model on only 24% of inputs and fails equivalence (R1). The complement still depends on model score, p=0.01 (R2). A few edges are removable and about 20% can be dropped without faithfulness loss (R3, R7).
relationships.display_finding: The circuit exceeded model performance on only 24% of inputs and failed equivalence; its complement retained dependence on model score at p=0.01, and about 20% of edges could be removed without faithfulness loss.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Stringent idealized tests: equivalence, independence, edge-level minimality
source_check.reason: R1–R3 and R7 show incomplete agreement, remaining complement information and redundant edges. These qualify circuit adequacy under stronger criteria that differ from the original operational definitions.

relationships.condition: IOI circuit in GPT-2 small, STR vs zero ablation, idealized tests

relationships.display_finding: Knockdown conclusions reversed between STR and zero ablation, while equivalence tests failed and the circuit's complement retained task information.

relation.reason: Own experiments directly evaluate IOI circuit faithfulness, localization, minimality and sensitivity to ablation choice.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates the existing IOI circuit with new statistical tests and reference distributions. Its criteria differ explicitly from the original subset-based tests despite retaining the task, model and logit-difference score.

source_check.notes: Table 1's caption reverses the rejection/retention interpretation supported by its cells and the surrounding text; the record's dismissal of the inconsistency as a misreading is too strong. IOI nevertheless clearly fails all three idealized tests; these differ from the original head-level criteria.
